o: We may halve (ceiling) up to op1 elements and subtract k from up to op2 elements (each element at most once per operation), minimizing the total. With n, op1, op2 ≤ 100, a knapsack-style DP over (index, op1 used, op2 used) fits easily: for each element choose to use neither, op1 only, op2 only, or both operations. When both are applied, doing subtract-then-halve (ceil((v−k)/2)) is at least as good as halve-then-subtract, but we take the min of both orders anyway.
k: State = (element index, op1 remaining, op2 remaining); four choices per element give O(n·op1·op2) ≈ 10^6 states-transitions.
Applying subtraction before halving never loses: ceil((v−k)/2) ≤ ceil(v/2) − k whenever the latter is valid.
Operations on tiny values can be wasted safely, so 'exactly' and 'at most' op counts coincide if we minimize over all used-op totals at the end.

a.i: dp[j][p] = minimum sum of processed elements having used j halvings and p subtractions. For each new value v, transition from (j,p) using none / op1 / op2 / both, rolling the array forward.
s: For each v compute half = ceil(v/2), sub = v−k (if v ≥ k), both = min(ceil((v−k)/2), ceil(v/2) − k if applicable).
Recompute dp descending over j, p combining the four choices.
Answer = min over all j ≤ op1, p ≤ op2 of dp[j][p].
a.t: O(n · op1 · op2) — at most 100 × 101 × 101 ≈ 10^6 transition evaluations.
a.sp: O(op1 · op2) — two rolling DP tables.

a.i: The same recurrence written as memoized recursion over (i, j, p) returning the minimal suffix sum; often easier to reason about and only explores reachable states.
s: Define solve(i, j, p): min sum of nums[i:] with j halvings and p subtractions left.
Try the four choices (skip, halve, subtract, both) recursively and take the minimum.
Memoize on (i, j, p); answer is solve(0, op1, op2).
a.t: O(n · op1 · op2) — each (i, j, p) state computed once with O(1) work.
a.sp: O(n · op1 · op2) — the memoization table (larger than bottom-up but simpler to write).

w: Bottom-up is preferable in interviews (less memory, no recursion depth concerns). Critical details: ceiling division (v+1)//2, the both-operations ordering (subtract first), guarding v ≥ k, and taking the min over ALL dp cells at the end (unused operations are legal). Edge cases: k = 0 (subtract does nothing but consumes op2 — the min-over-cells handles it), op1 = op2 = 0 (plain sum). Follow-up: reconstruct which operations were applied, or generalize to m operation types.
